messages.content: The report shows uncovered branches in the parser and cache adapter.
Keep the annotated line report and group the branches by changed module.
Should we raise the threshold immediately?
First distinguish a missing test from an unreachable defensive branch.
The parser branch is reachable for malformed headers.
Add a focused case for that header and retain the annotation as evidence.
The cache adapter branch depends on a fixture state.
Record the fixture state in the report so a later run is reproducible.
I will attach the report to the review.
Include the missing-line numbers and the test names that close them.
That gives us a useful recovery checklist.
Yes, use it as evidence rather than as a substitute for a stable gate.
The parametrized parser tests miss empty, unicode, and truncated inputs.
List those as explicit parameters with expected outcomes.
A single fixture currently hides which parameter failed.
Give each case an id and include it in the assertion output.
The invalid-header case also touches the fallback branch.
Keep that branch in the same matrix but explain its separate purpose.
One case passes locally and fails after the full suite.
Run it alone and after the neighboring cases to check state leakage.
The isolated run is stable.
Then preserve the isolated command in the review notes.
I have added the missing parameter ids.
Good; the report can now connect each edge case to its branch.
A database fixture leaves a temporary flag set for the next test.
Reproduce the order-sensitive failure with the smallest neighboring set.
The failure disappears when the test is run alone.
That points to shared state, not to a random assertion timeout.
The fixture uses module scope for speed.
Try function scope for the affected tests and reset the flag in teardown.
Function scope removes the order dependence.
Keep the isolated reproduction and the full-suite confirmation.
The annotated report now shows the intended branch.
Mention that fixture isolation was required before interpreting coverage.
I will separate the flaky issue from the missing-line issue.
That separation makes the recovery record much easier to audit.
After reset, a runtime test lost the default mock implementation and began failing.
Which layer had been responsible for installing that implementation?
A shared setup file had installed it for every test without documenting ownership.
Reset correctly removed the implementation, exposing the hidden dependency.
The first proposed fix only updated snapshots.
Snapshots can record the symptom; they cannot restore mock ownership.
We moved the needed implementation into each test or its beforeEach.
That makes the test owner explicit and keeps the setup local.
Cleanup now clears calls and restores replaced behavior consistently.
Good; each test owns what it needs and cleanup removes cross-test state.
The suite is stable without broad snapshot churn.
Record the ownership change as the resolution, with snapshots only as updated evidence.
An async matcher test sometimes finishes before the promise settles.
Await the assertion and make the rejection path explicit.
Another test uses a fake clock but never advances it.
Advance the clock at the point the scheduled callback is expected.
The fake clock is configured in a package setup file.
Keep the configuration narrow so unrelated tests use real time.
A timeout made the failure look like a matcher regression.
Capture the pending promise and clock state before changing the timeout.
The explicit await removes the intermittent pass.
Add a focused failure message for the unresolved branch.
The package tests now finish deterministically.
Keep the clock setup and async assertion in the test's ownership boundary.
The checkout journey currently locates the submit control with a brittle CSS chain.
Explore the visible name, label, and stable test hook before changing the test.
The control has an accessible name and a nearby form label.
Capture both candidates and note which one survives the responsive layout.
The generated trace shows the name is unique on the payment page.
Keep the trace as evidence and avoid committing an arbitrary DOM path.
A test hook exists on the confirmation action.
Compare its stability with the role-and-name candidate across the journey.
The role candidate reads more like the user action.
Prefer it when the trace confirms uniqueness and actionable feedback.
I will record the alternatives before migrating.
That discovery record will make later locator changes reviewable.
The migrated locator passes Chromium but fails in a WebKit journey.
Open the trace at the action and inspect the accessible tree in both runs.
WebKit exposes a duplicate label from a hidden dialog.
Scope the locator to the visible checkout region and rerun the trace.
The scoped role locator is unique in both traces.
Retain the before-and-after trace links in the migration note.
A test hook would also avoid the duplicate.
Use the hook only if the user-facing contract cannot remain unique.
The role locator still gives the clearer failure message.
Then make cross-browser trace validation part of the acceptance evidence.
The journey now passes on all selected engines.
Document the hidden-dialog cause so the locator is not widened later.
The account journey has three steps with different control markup by browser.
Assert the user-visible role or label at each step before considering a hook.
The first step has a stable role and the second has a stable label.
Keep those semantic candidates and capture a trace for each browser.
The final action has a dedicated test hook.
Use the hook there if the semantic name is localized or duplicated.
Firefox exposed a timing wait around the final action.
Wait on the action's enabled state rather than adding a fixed delay.
The trace confirms the action is enabled before the click.
Include that state transition in the journey evidence.
All three browser runs now agree on the assertions.
The stable journey should preserve the discovery and trace notes.
The deterministic integration build fails because the custom integrationTest classes cannot find a resource.
Check whether that source set still processes its test resources before changing application code.
The processTestResources dependency was removed from the custom task.
That explains why the resource is absent when the integration classes run.
The task also reports an old output directory as up to date.
Restore the task dependency and invalidate the stale output for that task.
After invalidation, resources are copied and the build fails no longer.
Keep the fix in build configuration; production code is not implicated.
A clean repeat reproduces the successful result.
Record the dependency edge and stale-output invalidation as the conclusion.
This is separate from test-slice selection.
Yes, triage the deterministic build failure independently from test semantics.
A controller test loads the whole application context for one serialization assertion.
Compare a narrow web slice with the full context and list the required collaborators.
The narrow slice needs one explicit service stub.
Provide that stub and keep the assertion focused on the HTTP contract.
A repository test currently includes unrelated web configuration.
Move it to the data-oriented slice and avoid loading web beans.
Startup time drops in both tests.
Check that the narrower context still exercises the intended boundary.
The assertions remain meaningful after the split.
Keep a note of why each slice was chosen.
The build configuration issue is tracked elsewhere.
Good; keep scope selection and deterministic build triage as separate records.

l1Memories.content: An older pytest policy required a uniform 100% line-coverage merge gate for every change. It is retained as historical context only and is superseded by the dated current policy.
Keep an annotated report with missing executable line numbers and the responsible test module; use it to plan focused additions and review residual gaps.
Give boundary inputs explicit parameter ids and expected outcomes so a coverage review can connect each branch to a readable case.
When a fixture can leak state, reproduce the smallest order-dependent set, narrow its scope, and verify the fix both alone and in the full suite.
Coverage artifacts should use a date and commit label, preserve branch annotations, and identify whether a line belongs to a changed module.
Start a parameter failure in isolation, then rerun adjacent cases to distinguish a bad expectation from shared fixture state.
A test that needs a special mock behavior should install it in the test or its beforeEach and leave cleanup to clear and restore state.
Await asynchronous matchers, make rejection paths explicit, and preserve the pending operation in failure evidence.
During locator discovery, record role and label candidates before a dedicated test hook; choose the narrowest candidate that expresses the user action.
A locator migration review keeps before-and-after traces, browser names, and the visible-region scope used to establish uniqueness.

As of 2026-08-20, the current merge gate requires overall line coverage >=85% plus no newly uncovered executable lines in changed modules. The older uniform 100% merge gate is no longer current; annotated 100% remains a focused gap-closure technique rather than the universal merge threshold.
Select the narrowest Spring test slice that exercises the intended boundary, provide explicit collaborators, and keep assertions tied to that boundary.
For a repeatable build failure, capture the task graph, resource output, and a clean rerun before changing production sources.

For a current Jest flaky failure, the package owner supplies a minimal reproduction or seed, fake-timer configuration, and isolated failing command; the CI owner supplies worker and environment evidence. Accepting a snapshot update alone is forbidden.
For browser journeys, wait on the action's enabled or visible state and retain engine-specific traces instead of adding fixed delays.
Custom integration source sets must process their resources before execution; stale task output should be invalidated when a missing dependency caused a deterministic failure.

l2Scenes.content: Coverage recovery begins by establishing an annotated report, then adding tests for uncovered branches, isolating flaky fixtures, and finally applying the 85% overall line-coverage plus no-new-uncovered-lines gate for changed modules. The report is retained as a continuous loop: inspect, add focused cases, stabilize fixtures, and recheck the gate.

The review traces a shared mock incident into local ownership, consistent cleanup, awaited async assertions, and narrowly configured fake clocks. Snapshot evidence is useful only after behavior and ownership are correct.

Phase one moves from brittle CSS toward role, label, and test-id candidates discovered from the visible page. Phase two validates the chosen candidate with traces and scopes it when hidden or duplicate controls appear. Phase three keeps cross-browser stable assertions, action readiness, and engine-specific trace evidence so the journey remains durable.

The scene separates narrow test-slice choice from deterministic build triage: inspect the custom source-set task graph, restore missing resource processing, invalidate stale output, and verify with a clean repeat before considering production changes.

l3Profiles.content: 偏好可复现、可定位的测试证据：先缩小失败范围，再保留报告、参数、轨迹或任务图；测试应拥有明确的夹具和模拟状态，异步操作要显式等待，浏览器断言优先表达用户可见语义。覆盖率、切片选择与构建排障分别记录，避免用表面结果掩盖根因。
